danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Længe den nat sad fyrstinde Marja ved det åbne vindue i sit værelse og hørte lyden af bøndernes stemmer, der nåede hende fra landsbyen, men det var ikke dem, hun tænkte på. Hun følte, at hun ikke kunne forstå dem, uanset hvor meget hun tænkte over det. Hun tænkte kun på én ting — sin sorg, som efter afbrydelsen forårsaget af nutidens bekymringer allerede syntes at tilhøre fortiden. Nu kunne hun huske den og græde eller bede.

Efter solnedgang var vinden lagt. Natten var stille og frisk. Hen imod midnat begyndte stemmerne at dø hen, en hane galede, fuldmånen viste sig bag lindetræerne, en frisk, hvid dugget tåge steg op, og stilhed herskede over landsbyen og huset.

Billeder fra den nære fortid — hendes fars sygdom og sidste øjeblikke — rejste sig ét efter ét i hendes erindring. Med tungsindig glæde dvælede hun nu ved disse billeder og afviste med rædsel kun det sidste — billedet af hans død — som hun følte, hun ikke kunne betragte, selv ikke i fantasien, i denne stille og mystiske nattetime. Og disse billeder trådte så klart og detaljeret frem, at de snart syntes at tilhøre nutiden, snart fortiden og snart fremtiden.

Hun huskede levende det øjeblik, da han fik sit første slagtilfælde og blev slæbt gennem haven på Lyse Bakker, støttet under armene, mens han mumlede noget med sin hjælpeløse tunge, rykkede med sine grå øjenbryn og så uroligt og sky på hende.

»Allerede dengang ville han fortælle mig det, han sagde den dag, han døde,« tænkte hun. »Han havde altid tænkt det, han sagde dengang.« Og hun genkalde sig i alle detaljer natten på Lyse Bakker, før han fik det sidste slagtilfælde, da hun med en forudanelse om ulykke var blevet hjemme mod hans vilje. Hun havde ikke sovet og var listet ned ad trappen på tå, og ved døren til orangeriet, hvor han sov den nat, havde hun lyttet. Med en lidende og udmattet stemme sagde han noget til Tikhon om Krim og dets varme nætter og om kejserinden. Han havde åbenbart villet tale. »Og hvorfor kaldte han ikke på mig? Hvorfor lod han mig ikke være der i stedet for Tikhon?« havde fyrstinde Marja tænkt dengang, og tænkte det igen nu. »Nu vil han aldrig fortælle nogen, hvad han bar i sin sjæl. Aldrig vil det øjeblik vende tilbage for ham eller for mig, hvor han kunne have sagt alt det, han længtes efter at sige, og hvor ikke Tikhon men jeg kunne have hørt og forstået ham. Hvorfor gik jeg ikke ind?« tænkte hun. »Måske ville han så have sagt til mig, hvad han sagde den dag, han døde. Mens han talte med Tikhon, spurgte han to gange efter mig. Han ville se mig, og jeg stod lige ved, uden for døren. Det var trist og smertefuldt for ham at tale med Tikhon, som ikke forstod ham. Jeg husker, hvordan han begyndte at tale til ham om Lise, som om hun var i live — han havde glemt, at hun var død — og Tikhon mindede ham om det, og han råbte: 'Idiot!' Han var dybt nedtrykt. Bag døren hørte jeg, hvordan han lagde sig på sengen og stønnede og udbrød højt: 'Min Gud!' Hvorfor gik jeg ikke ind da? Hvad kunne han have gjort mig? Hvad kunne jeg have tabt? Og måske ville han da have fundet trøst og sagt det ord til mig.« Og fyrstinde Marja udtalte højt det kærlige ord, han havde sagt til hende den dag, han døde. »Elskede!« gentog hun og begyndte at hulke med tårer, der lettede hendes sjæl. Nu så hun hans ansigt foran sig. Og ikke det ansigt, hun havde kendt, lige siden hun kunne huske, og som hun altid havde set på afstand, men det frygtsomme, svage ansigt, hun havde set for første gang helt tæt på, med alle dets rynker og detaljer, da hun bøjede sig ned mod hans mund for at opfange, hvad han sagde.

»Hvad tænkte han, da han sagde det ord? Hvad tænker han nu?« Dette spørgsmål trængte sig pludselig på, og som svar så hun ham foran sig med det udtryk, han havde haft, da han lå i sin kiste med hagen bundet op med et hvidt lommetørklæde. Og den rædsel, der havde grebet hende, da hun rørte ved ham og overbeviste sig om, at det ikke var ham, men noget mystisk og forfærdeligt, greb hende igen. Hun forsøgte at tænke på noget andet og at bede, men kunne ingen af delene. Med vidtåbne øjne stirrede hun på måneskinnet og skyggerne og ventede hvert øjeblik at se hans døde ansigt, og hun følte, at stilheden, der rugede over huset og inde i det, holdt hende fast.
»Dunjasja,« hviskede hun. »Dunjasja!« skreg hun vildt og rev sig løs fra denne stilhed og løb til tjenestefolkenes rum, hvor hun mødte sin gamle amme og stuepigerne, der kom løbende hende i møde.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: For a long time that night Princess Mary sat by the open window of her room listening to the sound of the peasants' voices reaching her from the village, but she was not thinking about them. She felt she could not understand them no matter how much she thought about them. She thought only of one thing—her sorrow, which, after the interruption caused by present concerns, already seemed to belong to the past. Now she could remember and weep, or pray.

After sunset the wind had dropped. The night was calm and fresh. Toward midnight the voices began to fade, a rooster crowed, the full moon began to show from behind the lime trees, a fresh white dewy mist started to rise, and stillness settled over the village and the house.

Images of the recent past—her father's illness and last moments—rose one after another in her memory. With mournful pleasure she now lingered over these images, pushing away with horror only the last one—the picture of his death—which she felt she could not contemplate, even in imagination, during this still and mystical hour of night. And these images presented themselves to her so clearly and in such detail that they seemed now present, now past, and now future.

She vividly recalled the moment when he had his first stroke and was being dragged by his arms through the garden at Bald Hills, muttering with his helpless tongue, twitching his gray eyebrows, and looking uneasily and timidly at her.

"Even then he wanted to tell me what he told me the day he died," she thought. "He had always thought what he said then." And she recalled in every detail the night at Bald Hills before his last stroke, when with a foreboding of disaster she had stayed home against his wishes. She had not slept and had crept downstairs on tiptoe, and going to the door of the conservatory where he slept that night, she had listened. In a suffering, weary voice he was saying something to Tikhon—speaking of the Crimea and its warm nights and of the Empress. He had obviously wanted to talk. "And why didn't he call me? Why didn't he let me be there instead of Tikhon?" Princess Mary had thought then, and thought again now. "Now he will never tell anyone what was in his soul. Never will that moment return for him or for me when he might have said everything he longed to say, and I—not Tikhon—might have heard and understood. Why didn't I go in?" she thought. "Perhaps he would then have said to me what he said the day he died. While talking to Tikhon he asked about me twice. He wanted to see me, and I was standing right there, outside the door. It was sad and painful for him to talk to Tikhon, who didn't understand. I remember how he began speaking to him about Lise as if she were alive—he had forgotten she was dead—and Tikhon reminded him that she was gone, and he shouted, 'Fool!' He was deeply depressed. From behind the door I heard how he lay down on his bed groaning and cried out, 'My God!' Why didn't I go in then? What could he have done to me? What could I have lost? And perhaps he would have been comforted and would have spoken that word to me." And Princess Mary said aloud the tender word he had spoken on the day of his death. "Dear-est!" she repeated, and began sobbing, with tears that brought relief to her soul. She could now see his face before her. And not the face she had always known and always seen from a distance, but the timid, feeble face she had seen for the first time close up, with all its wrinkles and details, when she stooped near his mouth to catch what he said.

"What was he thinking when he said that word? What is he thinking now?" This question suddenly came to her, and in answer she saw him before her with the expression on his face as he lay in his coffin with his jaw bound up in a white cloth. And the horror that had seized her when she touched him and realized that this was not he but something mysterious and terrible, seized her again. She tried to think of something else and to pray, but could do neither. With wide-open eyes she stared at the moonlight and the shadows, expecting at any moment to see his dead face, and she felt that the silence brooding over the house and within it held her fast.
"Dunyasha," she whispered. "Dunyasha!" she screamed wildly, and tearing herself from that silence she ran to the servants' quarters to meet her old nurse and the maids who came hurrying toward her.
